To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) unsupervised audio embedding can be achieved with a simple coincidence based objective, (ii) unsupervised clustering can be used to impose structure on these embeddings, and (iii), weakly supervised active learning can be used to consolidate categories into semantic classes.

(i) a coincidence based loss function is a useful alternative to contrastive loss for unsupervised learning and (ii) active learning can reduce the number of labeled examples required to reach a given performance by up to a factor of 20.

(i) a combination of self supervision and clustering leads to a new state of art unsupervised representation of sound, and (ii) a cluster based weak supervision strategy leads to a 20x reduction in the amount of labeled data required to train a classifier for a target semantic category.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of learning frameworks that can mimic human learning, and the application of these frameworks to the problem of unsupervised sound representation and recognition.
the problem of unsupervised learning in the context of audio representation and classification.
the question of how humans learn to recognize sounds, and how we can leverage this knowledge to build machines that are more human like.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed framework provides a new state of art unsupervised sound representation, and a 20-fold reduction in labels required to reach desired classification performance.

the proposed framework is able to learn a sound embedding and a clustering objective in an unsupervised way, while being able to consolidate the learned categories by actively soliciting weak supervision to reach a high classification performance.
we have demonstrated that a combination of coincidence based self-supervised learning with active learning can be used to learn to recognize sounds with minimal supervision.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our approach is a new way to learn audio representations with a minimal amount of supervision, and that we can use these representations to learn to categorize and recognize sounds with very little supervision.
our framework can be applied to any audio dataset to learn a new representation of the data that is more robust and better captures the semantics of the data.

we propose a novel approach to learning audio representations that is based on a notion of coincidence, which is a generalization of the idea of self-supervised learning and which is combined with a cluster-based active learning procedure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a learning framework that combines coincidence detection, categorization, and active learning can achieve state of the art performance in unsupervised audio learning.
a simple combination of unsupervised and weakly supervised criteria can lead to a substantial reduction in the amount of supervision required for learning to recognize sounds.
a learning framework that combines unsupervised learning, active learning, and clustering can achieve state of the art results on a challenging audio classification task with minimal supervision.
